strengths: The paper addresses a relevant open-domain table QA problem and proposes a practical training-free cascade that combines sparse retrieval, dense reranking, row filtering, and LLM-based query/table enrichment.

The empirical results are promising on NQ-Tables: CRAFT improves over strong trained baselines at R@10 and R@50, and the stage-wise ablations show that each retrieval stage contributes measurable gains.
The paper includes useful downstream QA experiments with multiple LLMs, several retrieved-table depths, few-shot variants, and token-count analysis for sub-table contexts.
The method is modular and potentially useful in settings where fine-tuning specialized table retrievers is inconvenient or infeasible.
weaknesses: The central claim of outperforming SOTA is overstated. CRAFT is substantially below THYME at R@1, and the paper should be more careful that its advantage is mainly at deeper recall and downstream QA, not uniformly across retrieval metrics.

There are troubling inconsistencies and wording errors in the analysis. For example, Table 4 reports LI-RAGE at 54.17 F1, yet the text says Mistral-Small-Instruct at n=1 with 50.26 already surpasses it. Such errors weaken confidence in the interpretation of results.

Reproducibility is only partial. The system depends on Gemini-generated table descriptions/query decompositions and OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, but it is unclear whether generated artifacts, exact model versions, API settings, costs, and caching will be released. Without these, reproducing the main results may be difficult.
The evaluation is narrow: all main results are on NQ-Tables, with no validation on other table QA benchmarks or domains despite claims about adaptability and dynamic tabular domains.

Efficiency claims are under-supported. The cascade uses several expensive components and proprietary APIs, but the paper does not report indexing cost, preprocessing cost, inference latency, API cost, or memory usage against trained baselines.

Some comparisons may be unfair or insufficiently controlled. Downstream QA comparisons mix retrievers, LLM sizes, prompt settings, and retrieved context formats; Table 4 compares CRAFT with larger instruction-tuned LLMs against older dataset-specific systems, making it hard to isolate the retriever's contribution.

The novelty is moderate. The method is a sensible engineering cascade of existing retrievers, embeddings, and LLM-generated metadata, but the paper does not clearly establish a new modeling idea beyond combining off-the-shelf components.

The robustness experiment uses LLM-generated perturbations and the method itself uses LLM-generated query expansion, so the setup needs more detail and controls to ensure the robustness gain is not an artifact of generation style or semantic overlap.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for NLP: open-domain table question answering where retrieval quality strongly affects downstream answer generation.
The proposed cascade is practically motivated: sparse filtering followed by denser semantic reranking is a reasonable design for balancing broad recall and expensive model use.
The paper includes useful ablations over retrieval stages, table descriptions, query decomposition, irrelevant-row reduction, and retrieval depth, which helps identify where some gains come from.
End-to-end QA experiments with several LLMs connect retrieval improvements to the final task rather than reporting retrieval metrics alone.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated or internally inconsistent. The paper claims to outperform sparse, dense, and hybrid SOTA retrievers, but CRAFT is worse than THYME at R@1 and only wins at R@10/R@50. Table 4 also states that 50.26 surpasses LI-RAGE's 54.17, which is numerically false.

The methodology is not sufficiently rigorous for the strength of the conclusions. Results are reported on essentially one benchmark, with only 919 unique test queries, and the robustness evaluation uses LLM-generated perturbations without validation that they preserve answerability or comparable difficulty.

Comparisons are not clearly fair. CRAFT uses Gemini-generated table/query expansions, OpenAI embeddings, and LLM-based prompting, while many baselines are trained or reported under different settings; some baselines use full 966-query results while CRAFT uses 919 unique queries.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper relies on proprietary APIs/models such as Gemini Flash and text-embedding-3-small but does not specify decoding settings, prompts for all generated artifacts in enough operational detail, generated metadata release, costs, versions, or random seeds.

The training-free framing is somewhat misleading: while no task-specific parameter updates are performed, the system depends heavily on proprietary LLM-generated descriptions, subquestions, and commercial embedding models. This is a substantial external resource, not a simple off-the-shelf retriever baseline.

The retrieval pipeline is confusingly described. Stage sizes vary between top 5000, top 1000, top 300, and top 100 mini-tables/tables, and some appendix text appears mistaken about which stage feeds which. This makes it hard to reconstruct the exact system.

The end-to-end evaluation lacks key controls: prompt variance, answer normalization details, statistical significance, latency/cost, and whether all retrievers are evaluated with the same table truncation, same LLM prompts, and same retrieved-context formatting.

The claimed practical efficiency is under-supported. The paper reports token reduction from sub-tables but not full retrieval latency, indexing cost, API cost, preprocessing cost for 169,898 tables, or comparison against stronger efficient rerankers.

Writing and presentation issues reduce confidence, including typos, citation inconsistencies, unclear table labels, and claims that do not match the numbers. These are not merely cosmetic because they affect interpretation of the results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical ACL/NLP problem: open-domain table retrieval and table QA without dataset-specific retraining. The motivation is clear, and the training-free framing is useful for domains where tables or schemas change frequently.

CRAFT is simple but effective: a cascaded pipeline combining SPLADE, SentenceTransformer reranking, OpenAI embeddings, LLM-generated table/query enrichment, and sub-table pruning. The staged design is well aligned with scalable retrieval practice.

The empirical results are promising. On NQ-Tables, CRAFT achieves the best reported R@10 and R@50 in Table 1 while remaining competitive with fine-tuned dense and hybrid table retrievers. The robustness experiment under paraphrased queries is also a valuable addition.

The paper includes meaningful ablations over table descriptions, query decomposition, row reduction, reranking depth, few-shot prompting, and sub-table versus full-table token usage. These analyses support several design choices rather than reporting only a final number.
The end-to-end QA results show that better retrieval translates into downstream gains across multiple LLMs, including smaller open models and larger instruction-tuned models.
weaknesses: The novelty is mostly system-integration novelty rather than a new retrieval model or learning method. The contribution is useful and sound, but the main-conference case depends on whether the community views this particular cascade as sufficiently distinctive beyond combining strong off-the-shelf components.

Reproducibility is only partial. Key components rely on proprietary or version-sensitive services, including Gemini Flash, text-embedding-3-small, and larger commercial or hosted LLMs. The paper provides prompts, but not enough detail about API settings, caching, generation variance, cost, or whether generated descriptions/sub-questions will be released.

Several claims are overstated or internally inconsistent. For example, Table 4 reports LI-RAGE at 54.17 and CRAFT with n=1 Mistral-Small at 50.26, but the text says the latter surpasses LI-RAGE. The conclusion that CRAFT outperforms all existing TQA systems should be softened given mixed R@1 results and limited benchmark coverage.

The comparison protocol needs clearer alignment. Some baselines appear trained/evaluated on NQ-Tables but may use the full 966-query test set, whereas CRAFT uses 919 unique queries; T-RAG is marked as full-test-set. This raises concerns about exact comparability, especially for small differences.

Efficiency claims are under-supported. The cascade filters 169,898 tables through multiple embedding and reranking stages and uses LLM-generated table descriptions/query expansions, but the paper does not report indexing cost, inference latency, API cost, memory, or throughput. Token-count reduction alone is not enough to establish scalability.

The robustness experiment uses Gemini-generated perturbations, which may not reflect natural user paraphrases and may favor a pipeline that also uses Gemini for query expansion. Human-written paraphrases or multiple perturbation generators would make the evidence stronger.

The evaluation is limited to NQ-Tables. Given the central claim of adaptability to evolving domains, cross-dataset experiments or at least zero-shot transfer to another table QA/retrieval benchmark would substantially strengthen the paper.

Presentation quality needs polishing. There are typos, grammar issues, table formatting problems, ambiguous descriptions of stage sizes, and some confusing appendix wording about which stage feeds which. These do not invalidate the work, but they reduce confidence in experimental care.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: scalable open-domain table retrieval and QA without task-specific fine-tuning. The motivation is clear and relevant to current retrieval-augmented QA systems.

The cascaded design is practically sensible: sparse high-recall filtering, dense mini-table pruning, and stronger embedding-based reranking. The method is modular and likely useful in settings where retraining specialized retrievers is costly.

Empirical results on NQ-Tables are strong, especially retrieval recall and downstream QA F1 when using the same LLMs across retrievers. The paper also includes useful ablations for table descriptions, query decomposition, row filtering, and reranking stages.
The mini-table idea is well supported by token-count reductions and end-to-end QA comparisons, and the case studies make the noise-reduction benefit intuitive.
The paper is transparent about an important OTT-QA limitation: end-to-end evaluation uses oracle passages and is not directly comparable to full open-retrieval systems.
weaknesses: The contribution is mostly an engineering composition of existing sparse retrievers, embedding APIs, LLM-generated descriptions, query expansion, and reranking. The paper would benefit from a sharper account of what is technically novel beyond pipeline assembly and model selection.

Reproducibility is a significant concern. The abstract says code and data are available but provides no link, and the core system depends on proprietary or version-sensitive services such as Gemini, OpenAI embeddings, and GPT-4o. Exact prompts are included, but API versions, decoding/settings, caching, generation failures, indexing details, and costs are not sufficiently specified.

Several comparisons are difficult to interpret. CRAFT uses modern proprietary embeddings and generated table/query augmentations, while many baselines are older or fine-tuned under different assumptions. The distinction between supervised SPLADE baselines and the base SPLADE used in CRAFT is noted but not analyzed enough to ensure a fair comparison.

The efficiency claims are not fully substantiated. The paper reports token counts and embedding-call reductions, but does not provide actual latency, wall-clock cost, API cost, memory, indexing time, or throughput. Some descriptions appear inconsistent about whether Stage 2 embeddings are precomputed or generated on the fly.

The OTT-QA end-to-end results are limited by oracle gold passages, so the paper does not demonstrate a complete multi-hop open-domain table-text QA system on that benchmark. This weakens claims about real-world open-domain multi-hop performance.

The robustness evaluation is narrow: perturbations are generated by Gemini rather than by human paraphrases or established robustness benchmarks, and the main comparison is against DTR rather than the strongest current baselines.

Some presentation issues reduce confidence: malformed table formatting, inconsistent CRAFT variants in reported results, missing code URL, grammatical errors, and occasional overclaiming such as describing results as SOTA where the evidence is conditional on model/API choices.

strengths: The paper addresses an important ACL/NLP problem: scalable open-domain table retrieval for table QA, with evaluation on NQ-Tables and OTT-QA.

The proposed system is practically motivated: a cascaded sparse-to-dense pipeline, table descriptions, query expansion, and mini-table construction are plausible ways to combine off-the-shelf retrievers without task-specific fine-tuning.

The retrieval results on NQ-Tables are encouraging, especially the reported R@1/R@50 gains over several trained baselines, and the ablations show that descriptions, query decomposition, row filtering, and reranking each contribute some benefit.

The mini-table idea is useful from an engineering perspective, and the paper provides evidence that compact table contexts reduce token usage substantially and can improve downstream QA compared with full-table contexts.
The paper includes multiple evaluation angles: retrieval recall, perturbed-query robustness, end-to-end QA, token-count analysis, ablations, and qualitative error cases.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. On OTT-QA, CRAFT is not state of the art at R@1 and mainly becomes competitive only at larger recall depths; the end-to-end OTT-QA evaluation uses oracle gold passages, so it does not demonstrate a full open-domain multi-hop QA system.

The novelty is limited. The system is mostly a pipeline composition of SPLADE, LLM-generated metadata/query expansion, sentence-transformer/Jina/OpenAI/Gemini embeddings, and LLM answer generation. The paper needs a sharper explanation of what is methodologically new beyond engineering a cascade of existing components.

Several comparisons are potentially unfair or confounded. End-to-end gains over prior work are mixed with stronger modern generators such as GPT-4o and 70B-class models, making it hard to attribute improvements to retrieval. The paper does not consistently compare all retrievers under identical answer generators, contexts, and prompting setups.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code and data are available but provides no actual link. The method relies heavily on closed/proprietary APIs and generated artifacts from Gemini/OpenAI; prompts are shown, but generated table descriptions, query expansions, model versions, costs, seeds, and exact indexing/reranking details are insufficient for reproduction.

There are internal inconsistencies and unclear implementation details. The description of Stage 2 alternates between reranking Stage-1 top-5000 tables and ANN search over all precomputed row embeddings; the claimed online embedding-call reductions are hard to reconcile with the described on-the-fly mini-table scoring. Some reported numbers also differ across tables/text, e.g. OTT-QA Stage-2 R@10 appears inconsistent.

The robustness experiment is narrow and not fully convincing: paraphrases are generated by Gemini, while Gemini/OpenAI-based components are also used in the system, and only DTR is used as the main robustness baseline despite stronger contemporary baselines being available.

The efficiency claims lack direct latency, memory, indexing-time, API-cost, and throughput measurements. Token-count reductions are useful but do not establish overall computational efficiency, especially given multi-stage querying and proprietary embedding calls.

The paper would benefit from stronger statistical and diagnostic support: no significance testing or confidence intervals are provided, and error analysis is mostly qualitative. The claim that CRAFT is robust and broadly adaptable remains under-supported.

Writing and presentation issues reduce confidence. Some sections are repetitive, some claims are imprecise, and there are grammatical/formatting problems. The baseline hyperparameter appendix appears to describe training configurations for baselines rather than the proposed training-free method, which may confuse readers.

Overall, the work may be a reasonable Findings-level contribution after revision, but in its current form unresolved concerns about fair comparison, reproducibility, and overclaiming prevent a clear positive recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in open-domain table QA: retrieving relevant tables from large corpora without dataset-specific fine-tuning. The motivation is clear and well aligned with current NLP/RAG needs.

CRAFT is a practical and well-engineered cascaded retrieval pipeline combining sparse retrieval, mini-table construction, dense reranking, and LLM-based answer generation. The modularity and training-free deployment story are compelling.

The empirical results are strong. On NQ-Tables, CRAFT achieves the best reported R@1/R@50 among the compared retrievers, despite most baselines being trained on the target dataset. On OTT-QA, it is competitive at higher recall thresholds, supporting the claim that the approach generalizes reasonably well.

The paper includes useful ablations for table descriptions, query decomposition, irrelevant-row reduction, reranking depth, mini-table vs full-table contexts, and few-shot prompting. These analyses help establish which parts of the pipeline contribute to performance.

The efficiency motivation is credible: mini-tables substantially reduce context length, and the cascade sharply narrows the candidate set before expensive reranking. This is practically relevant for table QA systems using LLMs.
weaknesses: The novelty is mostly in system composition rather than a new retrieval model or learning algorithm. Cascaded sparse-to-dense retrieval, query/table expansion, reranking, and row filtering are all established ideas; the contribution is valuable but somewhat incremental.

Reproducibility is only partially convincing. The method depends on proprietary and changing models such as Gemini, OpenAI text-embedding models, and GPT-4o, but the paper gives limited details on API settings, versions, randomness, cached generations, costs, or failure handling. The abstract says code/data are available but does not provide a visible link.

Several comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. CRAFT uses strong closed-source components and generated table/query descriptions, while baselines are trained retrievers with different assumptions. The end-to-end GPT-4o gains in particular conflate retrieval improvements with a much stronger generator.

The OTT-QA end-to-end evaluation uses oracle gold passages, so it does not demonstrate a complete open-domain table-and-text QA pipeline. This materially limits the strength of the claims about multi-hop or real-world OTT-QA performance.

The efficiency section would be stronger with actual wall-clock latency, indexing time, storage, API cost, and throughput measurements. The current analysis focuses on embedding-call and token-count proxies, which are helpful but insufficient for a system paper making scalability claims.

Some methodological details are unclear or internally confusing, especially around whether Stage 2 mini-table embeddings are precomputed or generated on the fly, how rows are selected for each query at scale, and whether all baseline numbers are reproduced under identical preprocessing/evaluation settings.

The presentation has polish issues: formatting artifacts, missing spaces, occasional grammatical problems, and dense tables that are hard to read. These do not undermine the core contribution, but they reduce clarity.
